FISHER
ON-SCENE COMMANDER
CETACEAN RESCUE SPECIALIST

A blank incident card floats in the dim light of the Undersea Archive. One phone call breaks the silence and begins a wait that will last almost twenty hours.

The player is the information coordinator for the joint rescue command. You receive reports, read back times, locations, and conditions for confirmation, maintain the shared log, and accurately relay instructions approved by the on-scene commander and cetacean rescue specialists.

TIME: Approximately 08:40 on April 19, 2022.

FISHER: It is off Banbianshan, about eight hundred meters from shore. On my way back, I saw a very large dark shape stuck on the shoal. It was still moving its tail. The blowhole is above the water, and I can sometimes see it exhale. There are shallow areas and aquaculture nets nearby. I will send you the location now.

Record the call time, location screenshot, caller's contact details, and exact words. Mark the unverified species, length, and injuries as “pending on-site verification.”

The caller reports a suspected stranded cetacean that is still active. This record can begin verification and rescue coordination, but it cannot by itself confirm the species, weight, injuries, or cause of stranding.

The advance team reaches the muddy tidal flat. Part of the whale remains in the water while the tide continues to fall, and onlookers begin to gather.

ON-SCENE COMMANDER: Separate the people from the working lanes first. No one is to stand in front of the head or behind the tail. Do not push or pull without specialist approval.

After the tide recedes, most of the whale's body is exposed on the tidal flat. Rescuers keep its skin wet and address visible wounds under specialist guidance.

Create hourly record rounds covering breathing regularity, body posture, visible abrasions, skin moisture, shade, and water supply. Attach a time and reporter to each entry. The player records only visible abrasions and vital-sign trends reported by the field team; unsupported claims of internal injury do not enter the log.

A single observation cannot replace continuous assessment. The player may not independently diagnose the whale, design a treatment plan, or order firefighters to increase water pressure. Record the original observations and refer the trend to specialists for judgment.

The tide begins to rise across the flat. The command interface opens four cards: tide trend, specialist assessment, towing formation, and offshore route. Waiting for the tide does not mean the work has stopped; every period of waiting contains preparation for the next step.

Check every pre-tow item: whether the tide can support the whale, whether specialists approve an attempt, whether buffered rigging is complete, whether the scout vessel has cleared aquaculture nets, and whether communications between vessels are working.

Public reports record different times down to the minute. This scene does not treat one reported timestamp as the only possible version. The towing plan must address the animal's condition, human safety, route obstacles, and limits on acceleration together.

Darkness reduces the world to deck lights and voices over the radio. Four sources remain: specialist instructions, rope-tension trends, the scout vessel's depth and net reports, and reports of the whale's breathing and voluntary movement.

Sort the reports by time. Request a read-back for any figure that lacks a timestamp or source, then submit a recommendation to continue, pause for inspection, or stop to the commander.

The towing vessel reports that the tension curve has turned amber and the whale is leaning to one side. The specialist team advises pausing acceleration to check the attachment points and body position. No single reading can independently decide whether the tow continues or stops.

As the vessels move farther from shore, the radio signal begins to break up. The scout vessel reports dense aquaculture nets ahead and recommends a course change; communications then become unstable for a time.

The log may retain “unknown.” A complete log does not need a number in every field, but every number it does contain should have a known source and time.

The vessels reach the planned release area. The specialist team orders forward movement to stop while they observe breathing, voluntary tail movement, and body balance. Once release conditions are met, the field team releases the whale from the tow.

The whale remains at the surface for a moment, then moves its tail and dives on its own. Public footage proves a visible condition at one moment; it cannot replace a medical examination or long-term tracking.

The player returns to the final page of the command log. The screen shows the initial report, on-site verification, life support, tow preparation, night navigation, and release from tow in sequence. Each point can expand to show its source, time, and approving authority.

ON-SCENE COMMANDER: Before your shift ends, list every item we did not confirm separately. The next rescue team needs to know what we were missing.

This rescue returned a living sperm whale to deep water. The available records cannot confirm whether it recovered in the long term from injuries caused by the stranding.
